@graph.headline: How to Write a Crypto Press Release That Gets Picked Up in 2026
@graph.alternativeHeadline: Structure, news peg, compliance language and the pitch email that actually earns tier-1 crypto coverage
@graph.description: Most crypto press releases die in the inbox because they bury the news peg, skip the compliance line, and send the same pitch to forty reporters. This 2026 guide covers the exact structure, the one-story rule, forward-looking statements language for token releases, wire vs direct-pitch sequencing, and what a 150-word pitch email looks like when it works.
keywords: how to write a crypto press release

itemListElement.name: How to Write a Crypto Press Release That Gets Picked Up in 2026

mainEntity.name: How long should a crypto press release be in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Between 400 and 600 words for the body, excluding the compliance block and boilerplate. Below 350 words you leave questions a reporter has to email you to answer, and most will not. Above 700 words you are padding and the journalist stops reading. The structure is: headline, dateline plus first paragraph with the full story, one or two body paragraphs, two quotes, a compliance line, and a boilerplate under 100 words.

mainEntity.name: What makes a crypto press release actually newsworthy?

acceptedAnswer.text: A hard, dated, verifiable fact that did not exist yesterday: a funding round with a named lead and a number, a mainnet launch on a specific date, a named exchange listing, a named partnership where both parties can be quoted, a regulatory milestone, or a significant on-chain metric crossed for the first time. 'Continued momentum' and 'exciting growth' are not news. If you cannot point to one specific event on one specific date, you do not have a release yet.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a compliance disclaimer in my Web3 press release?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for any release that touches a token, a raise, or any financial instrument. A forward-looking statements disclaimer and a line clarifying the release is for informational purposes and does not constitute investment advice are standard at financial desks. Their absence signals regulatory carelessness and is a reason for editors at Forbes, Bloomberg and the financial desks of CoinDesk and The Block to pass on your story or push it into a paid slot.

mainEntity.name: Should I use a wire service or pitch journalists directly?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both, for different purposes. Wire distribution on GlobeNewswire, PR Newswire or PRWeb (roughly $800 to $2,000 per release) creates a citable, indexed record and drives syndication to regional outlets in Korea, Japan and India. It does not land your story at CoinDesk, Cointelegraph or Decrypt, because those editors do not rely on wires as their primary source. For tier-1 pickup, you pitch each target journalist directly, by name, under 150 words, separately from the wire drop.

mainEntity.name: What should the pitch email that accompanies a release look like?

acceptedAnswer.text: One hundred to 150 words, addressed to one journalist by name, with a subject line containing the hard news fact and an embargo date if applicable. The body has: one sentence on why you are writing to this reporter specifically, two sentences on the one angle most relevant to their beat, one sentence on what you are offering (exclusive, early data, an interview), and your contact details. The release is attached or linked, not pasted in full. Do not CC other journalists. Do not follow up the same day.
